en.sup: Supplied in English. The Greek verb has no stated object; the work is meant.

01.r: Every builder's work, one by one.
01.n: The Greek puts 'of each' first in the sentence, before 'the work', for emphasis: no builder is passed over.

02.r: Marks the work as the builder's own.

03.r: What each one has built on the foundation.
03.n: Abbott-Smith's first sense is 'work, task, employment'. Here it means the result of the work, the building itself.

04.r: Open to view, no longer hidden.
04.n: Abbott-Smith gives 'open to sight, visible, manifest', and notes the phrase with 'become', as here.

05.r: What is now hidden will come to light.

07.r: Gives the reason the work will be seen.

08.r: A coming day on which the work is shown for what it is.
08.n: The Greek says only 'the day'. A day of judgment is the likely meaning; the DRC adds 'of the Lord' and the BSB capitalises 'Day', both interpreting.

09.r: The day will make the work clear for all to see.
09.n: Abbott-Smith gives 'to make plain, declare', and cites this verse.

10.r: Explains how the day discloses the work.

11.r: Fire is the setting or means of the revealing.

12.r: The fire that tests and reveals.

13.r: Something is laid bare in the fire.
13.n: Present tense, used of a certain future. The subject is unstated: it may be the day, revealed in fire, or the work. Abbott-Smith lists this verse under the general sense 'to reveal, uncover, disclose', of things.

14.r: Adds what the fire will do.

15.r: Again, every builder's work in turn.

16.r: Marks the work as the builder's own.

18.r: The quality of the work, not its size.
18.n: Abbott-Smith gives 'of what sort'. The Greek places 'what sort it is' before 'the fire', which our English moves after the verb.

19.r: Asks what the work truly is.

21.r: The fire that tests the work.

22.r: The fire alone will be the test.
22.n: Absent from the Textus Receptus, so the KJV has 'the fire shall try'.

23.r: The fire will put the work to the proof.
23.n: Abbott-Smith explains that the verb is used primarily of metals, to test, try, prove, and that the testing is done in the hope that it will prove successful. That fits a fire set to try gold and silver.

tr_note: The Textus Receptus lacks αὐτό, 'itself', so the KJV reads 'the fire shall try' where the ASV has 'the fire itself shall prove'.
